patient.name: Rajesh Varma
patient.setting: GP surgery, then renal clinic over the following years
patient.complaint: Abnormal kidney function found on routine diabetes bloods
background: Type 2 diabetes for 15 years on metformin
Ex-smoker; owns a newsagent in Harrow

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely cause' in a patient with diabetes or hypertension and a low eGFR, and questions on its complications: anaemia, secondary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism and bone disease.

points: Annual bloods: **eGFR 41**; it was 58 two years ago.
Feels completely well; no urinary symptoms.
Retinopathy on his last eye screen.

steps.lead: Rajesh feels fine, which is typical: CKD is often **found incidentally** and is defined by damage or reduced function for **3 months or more**.
With long-standing diabetes and retinopathy, **diabetic nephropathy** is the likely cause; his hypertension adds to it.
Rajesh's urine ACR comes back raised: **persistent albuminuria** is evidence of kidney damage on its own.

steps.q: Rajesh has proteinuria but no haematuria and retinopathy. Which cause is most likely?
steps.r: **Diabetic nephropathy**: proteinuria without haematuria and gradual decline, usually with retinopathy. IgA gives haematuria.

steps.title: Common causes of CKD
head: Cause
Clues
rows: Long-standing diabetes, retinopathy, proteinuria without haematuria

points: Eight years on: Rajesh's eGFR is **18**.

steps.lead: Rajesh now has **late features**: fatigue, pruritus, nausea, oedema and hypertension, with a high potassium and creatinine.

steps.title: Rajesh at eGFR 18
steps.text: Normocytic anaemia, low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH: **anaemia of CKD** and **secondary hyperparathyroidism**.

steps.lead: Rajesh's bones are at risk of **fragility fractures** from secondary hyperparathyroidism, and his vessels from calcification.
Rajesh's pallor, flow murmur and Hb of 96 are **anaemia from low EPO**; his metformin must stop at this level of kidney function.

steps.text: In CKD, **secondary** hyperparathyroidism has **low or normal calcium** with high PTH. **Tertiary** has **high calcium** with high PTH, after years of stimulation.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (early morning urine ACR) and staging questions using eGFR. Remember that CKD needs abnormal results on two occasions 90 days apart.

steps.lead: Rajesh gives an **early morning urine sample** for ACR: the first-line test for kidney damage.

visual.title: Urine ACR
visual.label: Rajesh 42
visual.caption: Above 30 mg/mmol: ACE inhibitor plus SGLT-2 inhibitor, whatever the diabetes status.

steps.lead: Rajesh's eGFR was 41 and then 39 **three months apart**, with proteinuria: that confirms CKD, and the proteinuria worsens his outlook.

steps.q: Rajesh's eGFR is 39 on two tests 90 days apart. Which stage?
steps.r: eGFR **30 to 44** is **G3b**. G3a is 45 to 59.

visual.title: CKD stage by eGFR
visual.label: Rajesh 39
visual.caption: Stages 1 and 2 count only with other evidence of kidney damage.

steps.lead: At eGFR 39 Rajesh is **stage 3b**; eight years later, at 18, he is **stage 4**, heading for stage 5.
Rajesh's **renal ultrasound** shows small kidneys on both sides; and his eGFR is checked fasting, as a big steak the night before can skew it.

steps.text: One low eGFR is not CKD. It could be **AKI** or dehydration. You need **two results 90 days apart** (or other evidence of damage).

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': ACE inhibitor (plus SGLT-2 inhibitor) for proteinuria, statin for everyone, iron before EPO for anaemia, phosphate restriction then sevelamer, and dialysis or transplant for end-stage disease.

steps.lead: Rajesh's ACR is 42 and his BP is 152/90, so he starts an **ACE inhibitor** and an **SGLT-2 inhibitor**, aiming below 140/90.

steps.q: Which is the best first antihypertensive for Rajesh, with ACR 42?
steps.r: With proteinuria, an **ACE inhibitor** is first-line: it lowers intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.

steps.lead: Rajesh also starts **atorvastatin**, and stops buying naproxen for his back.

steps.text: Treatment slows the fall but does not reverse it: CKD is **irreversible**.

steps.lead: Rajesh's anaemia is treated with **iron first**, then **SC erythropoietin**; his high phosphate gets dietary restriction, then **sevelamer**.

steps.title: Treating anaemia of CKD
nodes: Correct iron first (oral ferrous sulphate, or IV iron)
Transfuse only if Hb < 70 on renal replacement therapy

steps.text: **EPO does not work without iron.** The exam answer for anaemia of CKD with a low ferritin is iron first, not EPO.

points: At eGFR 9, Rajesh starts **haemodialysis** three times a week.
Listed for a transplant; screened for TB and other infections.
Two years later he receives a kidney from his brother.

steps.lead: Rajesh's **transplant** is definitive. He now watches for rejection, has yearly skin checks, and his gums are monitored on ciclosporin.
Rajesh does not have ADPKD, but if he did, **tolvaptan** could slow its progression.
Rajesh was referred to nephrology when his eGFR fell below 30; staging and his ACR guided every drug decision along the way.

science.exam: Science questions ask why CKD causes anaemia (low EPO) and bone disease (loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylation, phosphate retention), and how ACE inhibitors and SGLT-2 inhibitors protect the kidney.

steps.lead: Each year Rajesh loses more **nephrons**, so filtration, hormone production and fluid and salt balance all decline together.
Rajesh's failing kidneys make less **erythropoietin**, so his marrow makes fewer red cells: a **normocytic** anaemia.
Rajesh's kidneys cannot activate vitamin D or excrete phosphate, so his calcium falls, phosphate rises and **PTH climbs**.

steps.title: From CKD to bone disease
nodes: Low calcium + high phosphate → PTH rises (secondary)
Years later: autonomous PTH, high calcium (tertiary)

steps.q: Why does Rajesh need alfacalcidol rather than plain vitamin D?
o: His gut cannot absorb vitamin D
steps.r: **Alfacalcidol** is already 1-alpha-hydroxylated, so it does not need the kidney to activate it.

steps.lead: Rajesh's ramipril **dilates the efferent arteriole** and his SGLT-2 inhibitor narrows the afferent: both lower glomerular pressure and protein leak.

steps.text: Do not mix up the arterioles: ACE inhibitors **dilate the efferent**; SGLT-2 inhibitors **constrict the afferent** (tubuloglomerular feedback). Both reduce hyperfiltration.

mcq.q: What is the leading cause of CKD?
How long must kidney damage or reduced function last to define CKD?
Which result pattern fits tertiary hyperparathyroidism?
mcq.r: **Tertiary**: autonomous PTH, so high PTH **and** high calcium.

mcq.q: What is the first-line investigation for suspected CKD damage?
Which eGFR range is CKD stage 3b?
Which ultrasound finding is typical of CKD?
mcq.r: **Bilaterally shrunken kidneys** separate CKD from AKI.

mcq.q: Which drug is first-line for CKD with proteinuria?
mcq.r: **ACE inhibitor** (or ARB), plus an SGLT-2 inhibitor if ACR >30.

mcq.q: What must be corrected before starting erythropoietin?
Which non-calcium phosphate binder is used in CKD?
mcq.r: **Sevelamer**; calcium binders risk hypercalcaemia and vascular calcification.
Less **erythropoietin** from peritubular fibroblasts: normocytic anaemia.

prompts.q: What is CKD and what are its main causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: irreversible, 3 months, usually diabetes or hypertension.

points.p: Progressive, irreversible decline in kidney function
Damage or reduced function for 3 months or more
Diabetic nephropathy: leading cause, proteinuria without haematuria
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis
Glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease, obstruction

prompts.q: How does CKD present, and what counts as evidence of kidney damage?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: early CKD is silent; damage is in the urine or the biopsy.

points.p: Often asymptomatic, found incidentally on bloods
points.why: Most exam stems start with routine bloods.

points.p: High potassium, creatinine and urea
Late: fatigue, pruritus, nausea, oedema, hypertension, pallor
Damage: persistent haematuria, albuminuria or proteinuria
Hereditary kidney disease or biopsy-proven chronic GN

prompts.q: What are the complications of CKD?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: blood, bones, heart and electrolytes.

points.p: Anaemia from low EPO: fatigue, pallor, flow murmur
Hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia
Secondary then tertiary hyperparathyroidism, fragility fractures
points.why: Tertiary: high PTH with high calcium.

points.p: CKD-mineral bone disease including osteomalacia
points.why: Bone pain, proximal myopathy, waddling gait.

points.p: Cardiovascular disease and vascular calcification
points.why: IHD is the commonest cause of death on haemodialysis.

prompts.q: How do you tell secondary from tertiary hyperparathyroidism in CKD?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look at the calcium.

points.p: Secondary: high PTH with low or normal calcium
Tertiary: high PTH with high calcium
points.why: Autonomous glands after years of stimulation.

points.p: Tertiary: abdominal pain, constipation

prompts.q: How is CKD diagnosed and what is the first-line test?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ACR first; eGFR below 60 twice, 90 days apart.

points.p: Early morning urine ACR first-line
points.why: Urine dip is the confirmatory test.

points.p: eGFR < 60 on 2 occasions 90 days apart
Proteinuria marks a worse prognosis
Renal ultrasound: bilaterally shrunken kidneys suggest CKD over AKI
points.why: ADPKD and diabetes can keep kidneys large.

prompts.q: How is CKD staged by eGFR?

points.p: G1 > 90 and G2 60–89, only with evidence of damage
points.why: Normal eGFR alone is not CKD.

points.p: G5 < 15: established renal disease

prompts.q: What other tests and pitfalls matter when assessing CKD?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: formula names, false readings, transplant screening.

points.p: Cockcroft-Gault: age, gender, creatinine, weight for creatinine clearance
MDRD: Creatinine, Age, Gender, Ethnicity (CAGE)
Large muscle mass or red meat the night before skews eGFR
Pre-transplant screening includes TB testing

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of CKD and when do you start an ACE inhibitor?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the ACR number decides it.

points.p: Control diabetes and BP, target 140/90 (lower if proteinuria)
ACE inhibitor (ramipril) or ARB, especially with proteinuria
Diabetes: start if ACR > 3 (classically > 2.5 men, > 3.5 women)
points.why: Regular ACR screening in all diabetics.

points.p: ACR > 30 any patient: ACE inhibitor plus SGLT-2 inhibitor
Statin for all; avoid nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs
points.why: Cardiovascular disease is the main killer.

prompts.q: How are the anaemia and bone disease of CKD treated?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always iron before EPO; always diet before binders.

points.p: Iron first (oral ferrous sulphate or IV iron)
Then SC erythropoietin (darbepoetin alfa)
points.why: Transfuse only if Hb < 70 on RRT.

points.p: Low-phosphate diet first, then sevelamer
points.why: Calcium binders risk hypercalcaemia and calcification.

points.p: Vitamin D: correct deficiency (D2/D3); alfacalcidol for secondary HPT in ESRD

prompts.q: What is the definitive treatment for end-stage CKD and its key risks?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: transplant, dialysis first, drug side effects.

points.p: Kidney transplant is definitive
points.why: Acute rejection is commonest in the first few months.

points.p: Haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis before that
points.why: IHD is the commonest cause of death on haemodialysis.

points.p: Skin cancer risk 3 to 5 times higher after transplant
Ciclosporin: gum hypertrophy, hypertrichosis, nephrotoxicity
Tolvaptan slows ADPKD progression

prompts.q: Why does CKD cause anaemia and bone disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the kidney is an endocrine organ: EPO and activated vitamin D.

points.p: Less EPO from peritubular fibroblasts: normocytic anaemia
Loss of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation: low calcitriol, low calcium
points.why: Less calcium absorbed from the gut.

points.p: Phosphate retention suppresses calcitriol and stimulates PTH
Secondary then tertiary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease

prompts.q: How do ACE inhibitors and SGLT-2 inhibitors slow CKD progression?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the arteriole each one acts on.

points.p: ACE inhibitors/ARBs dilate the efferent arteriole
Reduce proteinuria and nephron loss, even if normotensive
points.why: Why they are used in normotensive proteinuric CKD.

points.p: SGLT-2 inhibitors constrict the afferent arteriole via tubuloglomerular feedback

glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease: kidney damage or reduced function lasting 3 months or more.
glossary.eGFR: Estimated glomerular filtration rate, calculated from creatinine, age and sex; used to stage CKD.
glossary.GFR: Glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter each minute.
glossary.ACR: Albumin:creatinine ratio on a urine sample; the first-line test for kidney damage.
glossary.Microalbuminuria: Small amounts of albumin in the urine, an early sign of kidney damage, especially in diabetes.
glossary.Proteinuria: Protein in the urine; a marker of kidney damage and worse prognosis.
glossary.Diabetic nephropathy: Kidney damage from long-standing diabetes; the leading cause of CKD.
glossary.Hypertensive nephrosclerosis: Scarring of the kidney's small vessels from long-standing high blood pressure.
glossary.Glomerulonephritis: Inflammation of the glomeruli, often causing blood and protein in the urine.
glossary.ADPKD: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease: inherited cysts that enlarge the kidneys.
glossary.ESRD: End-stage renal disease: kidney failure needing dialysis or transplant.
glossary.Cockcroft-Gault: A formula using age, sex, weight and creatinine to estimate creatinine clearance for drug dosing.
glossary.MDRD: An eGFR equation using creatinine, age, gender and ethnicity.
glossary.Erythropoietin: A kidney hormone that tells the bone marrow to make red cells.
glossary.EPO: Erythropoietin, the kidney hormone that drives red cell production; given by injection in CKD anaemia.
glossary.Darbepoetin alfa: A long-acting synthetic erythropoietin given by subcutaneous injection.
glossary.Ferritin: A blood protein that reflects iron stores; must be adequate before EPO works.
glossary.Normocytic anaemia: Low haemoglobin with normal-sized red cells.
glossary.PTH: Parathyroid hormone: raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and gut.
glossary.Secondary hyperparathyroidism: High PTH in response to low calcium, as in CKD.
glossary.Tertiary hyperparathyroidism: Autonomous high PTH with high calcium after years of secondary hyperparathyroidism.
glossary.Hyperphosphataemia: High blood phosphate because failing kidneys cannot excrete it.
glossary.Phosphate binder: A drug taken with meals to bind dietary phosphate in the gut.
glossary.Sevelamer: A non-calcium phosphate binder used for hyperphosphataemia in CKD.
glossary.Alfacalcidol: Activated (1-alpha-hydroxylated) vitamin D that does not need the kidney to work.
glossary.Calcitriol: The active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made in the kidney.
glossary.1-alpha-hydroxylation: The kidney step that converts vitamin D into its active form, calcitriol.
glossary.CKD-mineral bone disease: Bone and mineral problems in CKD: abnormal calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D, fractures and calcification.
glossary.Osteomalacia: Soft bones from poor mineralisation, causing bone pain, proximal myopathy and a waddling gait.
glossary.Vascular calcification: Calcium deposits in artery walls, raising cardiovascular risk in CKD.
glossary.Fragility fracture: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less.
glossary.ACE inhibitor: A drug such as ramipril that dilates the efferent arteriole and reduces proteinuria.
glossary.SGLT-2 inhibitor: A drug such as dapagliflozin that makes the kidney excrete glucose and protects against CKD progression.
glossary.Efferent arteriole: The small artery leaving the glomerulus; dilating it lowers glomerular pressure.
glossary.Afferent arteriole: The small artery bringing blood into the glomerulus.
glossary.Tubuloglomerular feedback: The kidney's reflex in which sodium delivery to the distal tubule adjusts afferent arteriole tone.
glossary.Haemodialysis: Filtering the blood through a machine, usually three times a week.
glossary.Peritoneal dialysis: Dialysis using the lining of the abdomen as the filter, with fluid exchanged through a catheter.
glossary.Ciclosporin: An immunosuppressant used after transplant; causes gum overgrowth, excess hair and nephrotoxicity.
glossary.Gingival hypertrophy: Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of ciclosporin.
glossary.Hypertrichosis: Excess hair growth, a side effect of ciclosporin.
glossary.Tolvaptan: A vasopressin receptor blocker that slows cyst growth in ADPKD.
glossary.Sodium bicarbonate: An alkali used to correct metabolic acidosis in CKD.

technique.stem: A 70 year old woman with long-standing hypertension has had increasing tiredness and itching for 6 months. Her eGFR was 26 mL/min/1.73m² four months ago and is 24 mL/min/1.73m² today. Renal ultrasound shows two small kidneys. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 158/92 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis with a stage: decide acute or chronic, then the eGFR band.
Low eGFR on two tests over 90 days apart, **small kidneys**, anaemia and high phosphate: chronic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: eGFR 15 to 29 = **CKD stage 4**.

elim: Stable over 4 months with small kidneys: not acute.
Stage 3b is 30 to 44.
Stage 5 is below 15.
RAS might cause CKD but the question asks the diagnosis and there is no ACE inhibitor trigger or bruit.

steps.x: **C. CKD stage 4.** Rule: 90, 60, 45, 30, 15: 24 sits in 15 to 29.

technique.stem: A 48 year old man with end-stage kidney disease from IgA nephropathy is on haemodialysis. He is being assessed for a kidney transplant. He was born in Somalia and moved to the UK 10 years ago. He has no cough or night sweats.
technique.q: Which infection is most important to screen for before transplantation?

steps.x: Pre-transplant screening: which infection reactivates with immunosuppression?
Heavy immunosuppression ahead, from a TB-endemic country, no active symptoms: **latent TB** risk.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Screen for **Mycobacterium tuberculosis** (e.g. IGRA).

elim: H. pylori is not a standard transplant screen priority.
Hepatitis E is not routine pre-transplant screening; hepatitis B and C are.
Strep. pyogenes is an acute infection, not latent.
Toxoplasma is more relevant in heart transplants.

steps.x: **C. Mycobacterium tuberculosis.** Rule: pre-transplant screening includes TB.

technique.stem: A 58 year old man has CKD stage 3a from hypertensive nephrosclerosis. He takes ramipril and amlodipine. His BP is 132/80 mmHg and his pulse rate is 70 bpm. His 10 year cardiovascular risk has not been calculated. He has no history of heart disease.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate additional medication?

steps.x: Additional medication in CKD.
BP already at target, already on ACE inhibitor; CV prevention is missing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: All CKD patients start a **statin**: **atorvastatin**.

elim: Aspirin is not for primary prevention.
BP is already controlled.
Ezetimibe is second-line to a statin.
Spironolactone risks hyperkalaemia with ramipril and is not indicated.

steps.x: **B. Atorvastatin.** Rule: every CKD patient gets a statin.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and an ACR of 48 mg/mmol is started on ramipril. Her BP is normal. Six months later her ACR has fallen to 22 mg/mmol.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which ramipril reduced her albuminuria?

steps.x: Mechanism of ACE inhibitor renoprotection.
Proteinuria fell even though BP was normal: a **glomerular** effect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Less angiotensin II → **efferent arteriole dilates** → lower intraglomerular pressure.

elim: Afferent vasoconstriction is how SGLT-2 inhibitors act.
Ramipril does not lower glucose.
Albumin reabsorption is not the mechanism.
ACE inhibitors do not affect liver albumin production.

steps.x: **B. Efferent arteriole dilatation.** Rule: ACE inhibitor = efferent; SGLT-2 inhibitor = afferent.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man with type 2 diabetes has routine bloods. His eGFR was 52 mL/min/1.73m² four months ago and is 49 mL/min/1.73m² today. He feels well. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: eGFR 45 to 59 on two tests more than 90 days apart, with albuminuria, is CKD stage 3a.

steps.x: Diagnosis and stage.
Stable eGFR under 60 for over 3 months, and raised ACR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CKD stage 3a** (45 to 59).

elim: Stable over 4 months: not acute.
Stage 2 is 60 to 89.
Stage 3b is 30 to 44.
eGFR below 60 with albuminuria is CKD, not normal ageing.

steps.x: **C. CKD stage 3a.** Rule: 45 to 59 = 3a; 30 to 44 = 3b.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has had type 1 diabetes for 25 years. She has proliferative retinopathy. Her eGFR has fallen from 78 to 51 mL/min/1.73m² over 4 years. Urine dipstick shows protein 3+ and no blood. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her chronic kidney disease?
practice.e: Long-standing diabetes, retinopathy, proteinuria without haematuria and gradual decline are diabetic nephropathy, the leading cause of CKD.

steps.x: Cause of CKD.
Microvascular disease elsewhere, proteinuria **without haematuria**, gradual decline.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Diabetic nephropathy**.

elim: IgA nephropathy causes **haematuria**, often after infections.
Lupus nephritis gives haematuria and systemic features.
Polycystic kidneys: family history, flank pain, large cystic kidneys.
RAS: bland urine, ACE inhibitor creatinine jump.

steps.x: **A. Diabetic nephropathy.** Rule: diabetes + retinopathy + proteinuria without blood.

practice.stem: A 73 year old man with CKD stage 4 has 3 months of tiredness and breathlessness on exertion. He is pale and has a soft ejection systolic murmur. His pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
practice.e: Normocytic anaemia with normal iron, B12 and low reticulocytes in advanced CKD is from reduced erythropoietin.

steps.x: Cause of anaemia in CKD.
Normocytic, normal ferritin and B12, low retics: **underproduction**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low EPO** from the failing kidney.

elim: Haemolysis gives high reticulocytes and jaundice.
Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis.
Ferritin is normal and MCV is not low.
Myelodysplasia is possible in the elderly, but CKD stage 4 explains it.

steps.x: **E. Reduced erythropoietin.** Rule: CKD + normocytic anaemia + normal iron = low EPO.

practice.stem: A 56 year old woman has been on haemodialysis for 9 years. She has 2 months of abdominal pain and constipation. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 142/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: After years of CKD-driven secondary hyperparathyroidism, autonomous glands cause high PTH with high calcium: tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

steps.x: Diagnosis of hypercalcaemia in a dialysis patient.
Long-standing CKD; calcium **high**, PTH very high, phosphate high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tertiary hyperparathyroidism**.

elim: Malignancy suppresses PTH.
Milk-alkali suppresses PTH and gives alkalosis.
Primary usually has **low** phosphate and no CKD background.
Secondary has low or normal calcium.

steps.x: **E. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism.** Rule: CKD + high PTH + high calcium = tertiary.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man has CKD stage 4 from diabetic nephropathy. He has aching bones and has had a wrist fracture after a minor fall. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which set of results is most likely?
o: Calcium high, phosphate high, PTH low
Calcium high, phosphate low, PTH high
Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high
Calcium low, phosphate low, PTH low
Calcium normal, phosphate normal, PTH low
practice.e: CKD reduces calcitriol and phosphate excretion, so calcium falls, phosphate rises and PTH rises: secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease.

steps.x: Predict the bone biochemistry in CKD.

clues: wrist fracture after a minor fall
steps.x: Fragility fracture from **CKD-mineral bone disease**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH**.

elim: High calcium with low PTH suggests malignancy or vitamin D excess.
That is primary hyperparathyroidism.
Low PTH with low calcium is hypoparathyroidism.
Normal bloods with low PTH do not fit CKD bone disease.

steps.x: **C. Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH.** Rule: CKD = secondary hyperparathyroidism.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman is found to have a creatinine of 310 µmol/L. She has no previous results. She has itching and nocturia. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 160/94 mmHg.
practice.q: Which additional finding most strongly suggests chronic rather than acute kidney disease?
o: Muddy brown casts on urine microscopy
practice.e: Bilaterally shrunken kidneys on ultrasound mark CKD; hypocalcaemia and anaemia support it. The other findings occur in AKI.

steps.x: Which finding says chronic, not acute?
No baseline; anaemia, low calcium and high phosphate already hint at chronicity.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bilaterally small kidneys** on ultrasound.

elim: Hydronephrosis suggests obstruction, often acute.
Hyperkalaemia occurs in both.
Muddy brown casts are ATN (acute).
Urea is raised in both.

steps.x: **B. Bilaterally small kidneys.** Rule: shrunken kidneys = chronic.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man with type 2 diabetes for 8 years attends his annual review. His eGFR is 74 mL/min/1.73m². He has no symptoms. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to detect early diabetic kidney damage?
practice.e: Early morning urine ACR is first-line for detecting kidney damage (albuminuria), screened regularly in all diabetics.

steps.x: Screening test for diabetic kidney damage.
eGFR near normal; damage would show first as **albuminuria**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Early morning urine ACR**.

elim: 24-hour collections are cumbersome and not first-line.
Biopsy is invasive and not for screening.
Ultrasound shows structure, not early albuminuria.
Microscopy looks for cells and casts, not albumin.

steps.x: **B. Early morning urine ACR.** Rule: CKD first-line test = ACR.

practice.stem: A 62 year old woman has an eGFR of 54 mL/min/1.73m² on routine bloods. She has never had kidney function tested before. She is well, with no urinary symptoms and a normal urine dipstick. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm whether she has chronic kidney disease?
practice.e: CKD needs an eGFR below 60 on two occasions 90 days apart (or other evidence of damage). Her ACR and dipstick are normal, so repeat the eGFR.

steps.x: Confirming CKD.

clues: never had kidney function tested before
steps.x: One low eGFR, no evidence of damage: not yet CKD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Repeat eGFR at 90 days**.

elim: CT adds contrast risk and no diagnostic value here.
Isotope GFR is rarely needed.
Biopsy is for unexplained or active disease.
Ultrasound does not establish chronicity of a single value.

steps.x: **E. Repeat eGFR in 3 months.** Rule: CKD = two results 90 days apart.

practice.stem: A 61 year old man with type 2 diabetes has CKD stage 3a. He takes metformin and amlodipine. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional medication?
practice.e: With an ACR above 30 mg/mmol an ACE inhibitor is started (plus an SGLT-2 inhibitor), because it reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria.

steps.x: Next drug in proteinuric CKD.
ACR 36 (>30), BP above target, no ACE inhibitor yet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ACE inhibitor: ramipril** (and an SGLT-2 inhibitor).

elim: A thiazide does not reduce proteinuria.
Doxazosin is a late add-on.
Furosemide is for fluid overload.
Spironolactone is a fourth-line add-on with hyperkalaemia risk.

steps.x: **D. Ramipril.** Rule: proteinuric CKD = ACE inhibitor first.

practice.stem: A 70 year old woman with CKD stage 4 is tired and breathless on exertion. She is not on dialysis. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment for her anaemia?
practice.e: Iron stores must be corrected first (oral ferrous sulphate, or IV iron if insufficient); erythropoietin works poorly when iron is low.

steps.x: Initial treatment of anaemia in CKD.
Ferritin 38 and transferrin saturation 12%: **iron-deficient**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Iron first**: oral ferrous sulphate.

elim: Transfusion is for Hb < 70 on renal replacement therapy.
EPO comes after iron is replete.
No macrocytosis or folate deficiency.
B12 is not low.

steps.x: **D. Oral ferrous sulphate.** Rule: correct iron before EPO.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with CKD stage 5 on haemodialysis has itching. He has followed a low-phosphate diet for 3 months. He takes calcium acetate. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 144/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
practice.e: With high phosphate despite diet and hypercalcaemia on a calcium binder, switch to sevelamer, a non-calcium binder that avoids hypercalcaemia and vascular calcification.

steps.x: Change in phosphate management.
Phosphate still high despite diet; calcium is **high** on a calcium-based binder.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Switch to a **non-calcium binder: sevelamer**.

elim: Bisphosphonates do not lower phosphate and are avoided in advanced CKD.
More calcium worsens hypercalcaemia and calcification.
Calcium carbonate is another calcium binder.
Vitamin D raises calcium and phosphate absorption.

steps.x: **E. Switch to sevelamer.** Rule: diet first, then sevelamer; avoid calcium binders if calcium is high.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with CKD stage 4 has a low adjusted calcium, high phosphate and a raised PTH. Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D level is normal. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypocalcaemia?
practice.e: The failing kidney cannot 1-alpha-hydroxylate vitamin D, so calcitriol and gut calcium absorption fall. Her 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal, so the liver step is intact.

steps.x: Mechanism of hypocalcaemia in CKD.
Liver step fine; PTH is responding; the kidney step fails.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Loss of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation**: low calcitriol.

elim: CKD reduces, not increases, urinary calcium loss.
25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal, so the liver is working.
PTH is high, so the glands are working.
Diet is not the main driver in CKD.

steps.x: **E. Reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylation.** Rule: CKD bone disease starts with low calcitriol.
